archetype.name: Game Manager (quick-game backup)
archetype.definition: A backup who wins by completing short, on-schedule throws, adding designed runs and avoiding turnovers. He rarely pushes the ball past the sticks and leans on the run game and the defense to carry the rest.

report.headline: A quick-game backup who kept Baltimore afloat, but his role hinges on Lamar's ankle
report.take:
Tyler Huntley is what he has always been: a short-area completer who keeps the offense out of trouble and does not stretch the field. His 78% completion rate (1st of 43) and +7.4 CPOE (3rd) look like a star's line until you see the depth. His intended air yards are 4.78, he throws 3.19 yards short of the sticks on average, and only 9.4% of his throws go into tight windows. Eleven of his 41 attempts were behind the line and 23 more were under 10 yards. He has thrown seven passes 10 yards or deeper all season.

The season is really one game. He took 48% of snaps in relief against Tennessee, then started at Atlanta with Lamar Jackson out with a sprained ankle. There he went 24 of 32 for 201 yards, two touchdowns and a rushing score, and Baltimore won outright as a 3.5-point underdog. That was a good backup start: +3.4 passing EPA, no turnovers, and a 1.6 rushing EPA from his legs. It also came inside an offense built for Jackson. The Ravens rank 6th in offensive EPA and 2nd in success rate and lean run-heavy (27th in pass rate over expected), so Huntley's job is to stay on schedule behind Derrick Henry.

The completion numbers hide some soft spots. His short throws have a 56.5% success rate but a -0.206 EPA. The failures are costly, and third down has been poor: -0.444 EPA and a 38.5% conversion rate with 5.8 yards to go on average. The middle of the field (six throws, -0.882) and Mark Andrews (eight targets, -1.174 EPA per target) have been dead zones. The good plays came from a handful of intermediate throws (+0.844 on seven) and from Rashod Bateman. The three sacks at Atlanta also fit his career pattern. His pressure-to-sack rate has ranked 41st or worse every season he has been charted, so holding the ball is a trait, not a fluke.

The career line explains the volatility. In 2021–2024 he posted negative EPA in three of four seasons and never cleared 6.23 yards per attempt. Then 2025 brought a 0.202 EPA and a 12.9 CPOE in four games. This year's version sits between those: accurate, safe and limited. He is a capable stopgap whose value is binary. Jackson is reported as "definitely doing better," with a target return of this Sunday, and the depth chart already lists Huntley as QB2.

strengths.title: Accuracy within a narrow window
strengths.body: He completes passes well above expectation, and that has carried across seasons rather than appearing out of nowhere. 2025 was 2nd in CPOE and this year is 3rd. The cause is partly the throw menu: screens and quick outs inflate completion rate. Still, beating expectation on those throws is a real, repeatable skill.

strengths.title: Designed runs fit the Ravens' scheme
strengths.body: Baltimore's run game is built around a mobile quarterback, and Huntley plugs into it. All four of his designed runs were successful, at 0.877 EPA a carry, and one went for a touchdown at Atlanta. Four plays is a tiny sample. But he has run for 135 to 294 yards in every multi-game stint of his career, so the legs are part of who he is.

strengths.title: No turnovers, ball protected
strengths.body: He has zero interceptions, zero fumbles lost and zero turnover-worthy plays. That is exactly what a backup in a defense-and-run offense is asked to deliver. His career interception counts (3–4 in five-game stints) say this will not stay at zero, but low aggressiveness keeps the risk modest.

concerns.title: Throws short of the sticks
concerns.body: His average throw lands more than three yards short of the first-down marker, and on third down it shows: negative EPA and conversions under 40%. This is the cost of his style, not bad luck. A quick-game quarterback with a 6.44 yards-per-attempt ceiling needs the run game to set up short third downs. It will persist.

concerns.title: Takes sacks, career-long
concerns.body: He was sacked three times at Atlanta, and 13.3% of his dropbacks end in a hit or sack. He has ranked poorly in pressure-to-sack rate every charted season, including 49th in 2025. His three scrambles have gone for 13 yards and no first downs, so extending plays is not paying for the sacks. This is a real flaw, and it matters most against a good pass rush.

concerns.title: Middle of field and Andrews
concerns.body: Throws over the middle (six plays, -0.882 EPA) and targets to Mark Andrews (eight, -1.174 EPA per target) have sunk drives. Bateman, by contrast, has been worth nearly a point per target. On samples this small it is a hint about chemistry rather than a verdict, but it narrows where he can go with the ball.

trend.note: He went from a nine-attempt relief outing against Tennessee to a full, turnover-free start and an outright road win at Atlanta's 7th-ranked defense. Two games is very little to go on, and the trajectory ends the moment Jackson is cleared.

nextGame.headline: Only matters if Lamar sits; Cleveland's pass defense is the problem
nextGame.body:
If Huntley starts at Cleveland, he faces a defense built to punish his weaknesses. The Browns rank 4th in pass EPA allowed and 5th in sack rate, a bad pairing for a quarterback with a career habit of taking sacks. They allow 0.25 EPA on deep throws (13th), but that hardly matters for someone who almost never throws deep. The opening is on the ground: Cleveland is 29th against the run and dead last in explosive runs allowed. That points to a script where Henry and the designed runs carry the game and Huntley is asked to throw 25 to 30 short passes. Cleveland's offense is 31st in rush EPA and 25th overall, so a low-scoring, Ravens-ahead game at a 40.5 total is the likely shape. That again limits his passing volume.

Availability decides everything. Jackson was listed Out as of the 12th but is "definitely doing better," with an estimated return this Sunday. The depth chart already has Huntley at QB2. If Jackson plays, Huntley is a non-factor. On the line, center Cam Jurgens (100% of snaps) is in the "finishing stages" of concussion protocol. His return would steady protection against a strong sack unit. On Cleveland's side, defensive tackles Mason Graham and Mike Hall Jr. are both out. That thins the interior push and helps both the Ravens' run game and Huntley's quick throws. Linebacker Carson Schwesinger (100% snaps, ankle) is questionable; his absence would soften the short middle, where Huntley has struggled.

keyMatchups.title: Browns' pass rush vs his sack habit
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland gets home on 8.2% of dropbacks, 5th in the league, and hits quarterbacks at the 9th-best rate. Huntley holds the ball and ranks 23rd in sack rate this year. Without Graham and Hall inside, the pressure has to come off the edge, which his quick game can partly beat.

keyMatchups.title: Ravens' run game vs a leaky front
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland's run defense ranks 29th in EPA and 32nd in explosive runs allowed. Baltimore will lean on Henry and quarterback designed runs, and that shrinks Huntley's passing volume while lifting his rushing share. This is the most reliable part of the matchup.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end targets into a strong spot
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland holds top tight ends to -0.19 EPA per target, 3rd-stingiest in the league. Huntley's Andrews targets have already been his worst. Expect his efficient looks to go to Bateman and the backs, not the seam.

nextGame.watch: Lamar Jackson's practice status this week. If he is cleared, Huntley goes back to the bench; if not, watch how quickly Huntley gets the ball out against Cleveland's edge rush.

restOfSeason.body:
The most likely path is that Huntley returns to QB2 this week or soon after and is a spot-duty quarterback the rest of the way. In any further starts, expect what the career says. Completions will stay high because of the throw menu, and yards per attempt will sit in the low 6s. A few designed-run touchdowns are possible. He will take more sacks than a starter should and throw an interception every few games, because the zero won't hold.

The 2025-style efficiency (0.202 EPA a play) is the high end, not the baseline. His run of 0.08 to 0.20 EPA owes a lot to Baltimore's line, run game and receivers rather than a new level of play. Red-zone touchdown efficiency on six plays will regress. The CPOE and the low turnover rate are the parts most likely to last.
swingFactors: Lamar Jackson's ankle and return date
Opponent pass-rush quality, given his sack tendency

confidence.note: Two games, one of them a partial relief outing, and he is listed QB2 with Jackson's return possibly days away.
